why: An FDE is the person sitting in the room when the customer's security team returns a pentest report two weeks before go-live, and the deployment either survives that meeting or slips a quarter. You will be deploying your own code inside someone else's VPC, against their SSO, holding their regulated data, which means you personally own the authorization boundary, the secrets, and the answer to 'can tenant A see tenant B'. Reading the OWASP list is worthless here - you need to have actually exploited broken object-level authorization and a forged JWT with your own hands, because that is the only way you can look at a customer's API and see the bug before their auditor does.
prerequisites: Auth (topic 27): OAuth2 authorization-code flow, OIDC id_token vs access_token, JWT structure and claims (iss, aud, exp, sub), and how RBAC claims get into a request context - you cannot attack what you cannot draw.

Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems (topic 30): tenant_id propagation, Postgres row-level security, PII classification and audit trails, since most real findings in an FDE deployment are authorization findings, not memory-corruption findings.

FastAPI in production (topic 26) and PostgreSQL at depth (topic 29): dependency injection for auth, parameterised queries via bound parameters, and enough SQL to know why string interpolation into a WHERE clause is the whole bug.
Networking (topic 2): TLS handshake and certificate validation, HTTP request/response structure, headers, redirects, and proxies - you will spend ten hours reading raw HTTP in an intercepting proxy.
CI/CD and supply chain (topic 18): a pipeline you can add jobs to, plus SBOM/scanning concepts, because half of A06 is a CI problem rather than a code problem.

A local runnable copy of your own stack - Dokeo (Python/FastAPI/Postgres) and DefenderMate (TypeScript/Next.js) - with seeded data for at least two tenants and three roles, because the deliverable requires finding a real issue in your own code.

subtopics.name: Burp workbench: proxy, CA cert, scope, Repeater loop
subtopics.learn: Install Burp Suite Community, install its CA certificate into the browser trust store, and set target scope so Proxy history is not drowned in telemetry noise. Learn the loop you will run 200 times today: intercept a request, send it to Repeater with Ctrl+R, mutate one parameter, resend, diff status code / Content-Length / response time. Know Intruder's Sniper and Cluster bomb modes and that Community throttles Intruder hard, so scripted requests with Python plus `requests` are often faster for enumeration. Configure match-and-replace rules to swap the session cookie or Authorization header automatically - that is how you test cross-tenant access without re-logging in every request.

resource.label: PortSwigger: Burp Suite desktop documentation

subtopics.name: Map your own attack surface before touching a lab
subtopics.learn: Produce the artifact everything else hangs off: an endpoint inventory for Dokeo and DefenderMate with, per route, the HTTP method, whether authentication is required, which role/permission is checked, whether the object is tenant-scoped, what user input reaches a query/filesystem/HTTP client, and what it returns. Pull it from the OpenAPI schema plus route decorators rather than memory, and mark every route where the authorization check is 'the ORM filter happens to include tenant_id'. Also map trust boundaries: browser to edge, edge to API, API to Postgres, API to model provider, and any background worker that runs with elevated credentials. Every finding you produce later will be a cell in this table.

resource.label: OWASP WSTG: Identify Application Entry Points (WSTG-INFO-06)

subtopics.name: A01 Broken Access Control: IDOR and horizontal privilege escalation
subtopics.learn: Work the PortSwigger access-control labs end to end: unprotected admin functionality, admin functionality found via robots.txt or a JS bundle, user role controlled by a request parameter or a cookie, user ID controlled by a request parameter with and without an unpredictable GUID, and the 'user ID leaked in a redirect / in a different response' variants. The mechanism to internalise is that authentication answers 'who are you' and authorization answers 'may you touch this object', and almost every real breach is the second check missing on one route out of 200. Learn to test by identity swap: capture request R as user A, replay it verbatim with user B's session, and treat any 200 that should be 403 as a finding. Note that 404-instead-of-403 is a defensible design choice but only when it is deliberate and uniform.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Access control vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: API authorization: BOLA, BFLA, mass assignment, excessive data exposure
subtopics.learn: Learn the API-specific shape of A01 from the OWASP API Security Top 10: Broken Object Level Authorization (`GET /documents/{id}` with no tenant predicate), Broken Function Level Authorization (`POST /admin/users` reachable because the router guard was only applied to the GET), Broken Object Property Level Authorization / mass assignment (a Pydantic model or JS object spread that lets a client set `role`, `tenant_id`, `is_admin` or `credits`), and excessive data exposure where the API returns the whole ORM row and the frontend hides fields. Fix patterns matter more than exploits here: explicit response models with an allowlist of fields, separate input schemas that physically cannot carry privileged fields, and a single `authorize(actor, action, resource)` chokepoint rather than per-route ad hoc `if`. Then re-derive the same bugs against your own OpenAPI spec.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks 2023 (BOLA, BOPLA, BFLA)

subtopics.name: A07 Authentication failures: brute force, enumeration, reset flows, MFA bypass
subtopics.learn: Run the authentication labs: username enumeration via subtly different responses and via response timing, password brute-force with IP-lockout bypasses (X-Forwarded-For, alternating valid logins), 2FA bypassed by skipping the second-step request, and password reset poisoning via a spoofed Host header used to build the reset link. The general lesson is that authentication is a state machine and attackers move between states out of order - test every step for 'what if I just call step 3 directly'. Know the correct defences concretely: constant-time comparisons, uniform error messages and timings, Argon2id or bcrypt with real cost parameters (never SHA-256 of a password), single-use time-bounded reset tokens generated by a CSPRNG and stored hashed, and rate limits keyed on account plus IP plus device rather than IP alone.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Authentication vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: JWT attacks: alg confusion, unverified signatures, jwk/jku/kid injection
subtopics.learn: Complete the JWT labs with Burp's JWT Editor: unverified signature, `alg: none`, brute-forced weak HMAC secret (hashcat mode 16500 against a short `secret`), signature bypass via an embedded `jwk` header, via `jku` pointing at an attacker-hosted JWKS, via `kid` path traversal to a known file such as `/dev/null`, and RS256-to-HS256 algorithm confusion where the public key is used as the HMAC key. In code, know the difference between `jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False})`, decoding without pinning `algorithms=['RS256']`, and decoding without checking `aud`, `iss` and `exp` - each is a separate real bug and the last one is why a staging token can work in production. Then grep your own codebase and your customer-facing SDK for every decode call and check all four properties.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: JWT attacks

subtopics.name: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC implementation flaws
subtopics.learn: Work the OAuth labs: authentication bypass via a flawed `state` parameter (CSRF on the callback, linking the victim's account to the attacker's identity), stealing an access token via an over-permissive `redirect_uri` (open redirect chained to the callback, path traversal in the redirect, or a naive `startswith` check), and unprotected dynamic client registration. Understand precisely why `redirect_uri` must be matched exactly against a registered allowlist, why implicit flow leaks tokens in the URL fragment and referer, why PKCE (`code_challenge` S256) exists for public clients, and why an access token is not proof of identity - only a validated `id_token` with checked `aud`, `iss`, `nonce` and signature is. This is the highest-frequency FDE integration and the place where a customer's IdP config will hand you a real finding.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: OAuth 2.0 authentication vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: Sessions, cookie attributes and CSRF
subtopics.learn: Do the CSRF labs: no token, token not tied to session, token validated only when present, token in a cookie (double-submit done wrong), and SameSite Lax bypass via a GET-based state change or a client-side redirect. Get the cookie flags exactly right rather than approximately: `HttpOnly` blocks JS theft, `Secure` blocks plaintext transmission, `SameSite=Lax` is the browser default and still allows top-level GET navigation, `SameSite=None` requires `Secure`, and the `__Host-` prefix pins a cookie to one origin with no `Domain` attribute. Know when CSRF is genuinely not exploitable (a pure `Authorization: Bearer` API with no ambient cookie) and when engineers wrongly assume it isn't, and know that a strict CORS policy is not a CSRF defence because the simple request still fires.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

subtopics.name: A03 Injection: SQL injection by hand, then the correct fix
subtopics.learn: Run the SQLi track: UNION-based data extraction (determine column count with ORDER BY / NULL padding, find a text-compatible column, exfiltrate `information_schema.tables` on Postgres), blind boolean-based, blind time-based with `pg_sleep()`, and error-based via `CAST(... AS int)`. Then write the fix and prove it: bound parameters (`cursor.execute(sql, (value,))`, SQLAlchemy `text()` with `:param`), understanding that parameterisation binds values only - table names, column names and `ORDER BY` direction must be validated against an allowlist because they cannot be bound. Learn why ORMs are not automatically safe (`.filter(text(f"..."))`, `raw()`, string-built `IN` clauses) and why a WAF regex is a mitigation, not a fix. Finish by adding a least-privilege database role so even a successful injection cannot `DROP` or read another schema.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: SQL injection

subtopics.name: Injection beyond SQL: OS command, template, NoSQL, and LLM-adjacent sinks
subtopics.learn: Do the OS command injection labs (blind detection with `; sleep 10`, out-of-band via DNS) and the server-side template injection labs (identify the engine with `${7*7}` / `{{7*7}}`, then escalate through Python object attributes such as `__class__.__mro__` to reach `os.system` in Jinja2). The generalisation to carry: every injection is 'attacker data crossing into an interpreter', so enumerate your interpreters - shell, template engine, SQL, MongoDB query documents, YAML/pickle loaders, XPath, and now the model prompt itself. Fixes are structural: `subprocess.run([...], shell=False)` with an argument list, never `shell=True` with an f-string; sandboxed or logic-less templates; and `yaml.safe_load` over `yaml.load`. Cross-reference guardrails and prompt injection (topic 51) so you can explain to a customer why prompt injection is untrusted-input-into-an-interpreter with no parameterised query available.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: OS command injection

subtopics.name: XSS: reflected, stored, DOM-based, and a CSP that actually helps
subtopics.learn: Work reflected, stored and DOM XSS labs including a `document.write`/`innerHTML` sink reached from `location.hash`, and at least one context-escape lab (inside an attribute, inside a JS string, inside a template literal) so you internalise that escaping is context-dependent, not a single `escape()` call. Know the real fixes: contextual output encoding by the framework (React's JSX escaping, and precisely why `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` and Angular's bypass functions defeat it), DOMPurify for HTML you must render, and a Content-Security-Policy without `unsafe-inline` using nonces or hashes plus `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`. Understand what XSS actually buys an attacker in your app: it runs in the victim's origin, so `HttpOnly` protects the cookie but not the session - the attacker just issues authenticated requests from the page.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-site scripting

subtopics.name: SSRF and cloud metadata: the FDE's most dangerous feature request
subtopics.learn: Run the SSRF labs: basic SSRF to an internal admin interface, blacklist bypasses (alternate IP encodings, `127.1`, decimal integers, `localhost` variants, double URL-encoding), whitelist bypasses using the `@` userinfo trick, `#` fragments and DNS names that resolve to loopback, plus SSRF via the Referer header and via an open redirect chain. Then connect it to cloud reality: any 'give us a URL and we will import it' feature is one bad parse away from reading `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` and exfiltrating the instance role. The fix set is architectural - enforce IMDSv2 (token-required, hop limit 1), resolve the hostname yourself and validate the resulting IP against RFC1918/link-local/loopback ranges before connecting, re-validate after every redirect, and egress through a locked-down proxy with an allowlist rather than trusting a regex.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)

subtopics.name: XXE, deserialization and file upload
subtopics.learn: Complete the XXE labs (file retrieval via an external entity, blind XXE via out-of-band DNS/HTTP and via error messages, XInclude when you cannot control the whole document) and know the one-line fix: disable DTD processing and external entity resolution in the parser - in Python use `defusedxml`, never bare `xml.etree` on untrusted input. Do at least one insecure deserialization lab and be able to state why `pickle.loads`, `yaml.load` and Java native deserialization on attacker data are remote code execution by design, not by bug. Then the file upload track: web-shell upload via a bypassed content-type check, extension blacklist bypass, and path traversal in the filename. Fixes to be able to write from memory: allowlist by sniffed content type, generate your own filename (never trust `filename`), store outside the web root or in object storage, and serve with `Content-Disposition: attachment` plus `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: XML external entity (XXE) injection

subtopics.name: A05 Security misconfiguration: CORS, headers, debug surface
subtopics.learn: Do the CORS labs and be able to explain the exact failure: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` reflected from the request `Origin` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is a cross-origin data read of every authenticated endpoint, and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null` is trivially forged from a sandboxed iframe. This is the single most common FDE-introduced bug because it is what you type at 11pm to unblock a customer's frontend. Then sweep the rest of A05 on your own deployment: `/docs` and `/openapi.json` exposed in production, DEBUG mode returning stack traces and settings, default credentials on a bundled Grafana or Redis, directory listing, missing `Strict-Transport-Security` / `X-Content-Type-Options` / `X-Frame-Options` or `frame-ancestors`, and verbose version banners. Use the OWASP Secure Headers project as the checklist and check the response headers of your own production URL right now.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)

subtopics.name: Business logic flaws and abuse of legitimate functionality
subtopics.learn: Work the logic-flaw labs: excessive trust in client-side controls (a price or quantity in the request body), negative or overflowing quantities, inconsistent handling of the same value across two endpoints, flawed enforcement of workflow sequence, and authentication bypass via an email-domain check that trusts a user-supplied field. These are the findings a scanner will never produce and the ones customers care most about, because they map directly to money and to regulated actions. In an AI deployment the equivalents are concrete: an unmetered endpoint that lets one tenant burn the whole model budget, a job-submission API with no per-tenant concurrency cap, and a 'retry' button with no idempotency key that double-charges. Test by asking 'what does this endpoint assume, and can I violate that assumption while staying inside the API contract'.

resource.label: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Business logic vulnerabilities

subtopics.name: A02 Cryptographic failures and the secrets you actually hold
subtopics.learn: Audit data in transit and at rest rather than reading crypto theory: is TLS terminated at the edge and then plaintext HTTP inside the mesh, is `verify=False` set anywhere in an HTTP client, are database and Redis connections using TLS, is `sslmode=require` (which does not verify the certificate) mistaken for `verify-full`. On storage: passwords under Argon2id/bcrypt with per-user salts, tokens and API keys stored as hashes so a database dump is not a credential dump, envelope encryption with KMS for column-level PII, and a documented key rotation path. Know the anti-patterns by name - ECB mode, a static IV, `Math.random()` or `random` instead of `secrets.token_urlsafe`, home-rolled `==` comparison of MACs instead of `hmac.compare_digest`, and JWTs used as long-lived opaque session tokens with no revocation.

resource.label: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: Cryptographic Storage

subtopics.name: A06 Vulnerable and outdated components in your own supply chain
subtopics.learn: Run real scanners against your real repos rather than reading about SCA: `pip-audit` against the resolved lockfile, `npm audit --omit=dev` against DefenderMate, and `trivy image` against both container images to catch OS-level CVEs the language tools never see. Learn to triage instead of panic - is the vulnerable function reachable from your code path, is it a dev-only dependency, is there a fixed version and does it break your API - and to record that reasoning, because a customer's security team will ask why a HIGH is still open. Wire Dependabot or Renovate with grouped update PRs so the fix path exists before the finding arrives, and pin by digest in Dockerfiles so a nightly rebuild cannot silently pull a new base layer. Keep an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) as an artifact of every build so 'are we affected by CVE-X' takes minutes, not days.

resource.label: pip-audit (PyPA official repository)

subtopics.name: Security testing in CI: SAST, DAST and a gate policy people won't disable
subtopics.learn: Add three jobs and, crucially, decide what each one blocks. SAST with Semgrep or CodeQL on every PR, using a curated ruleset plus custom rules for your own footguns (any `jwt.decode` without `algorithms=`, any ORM query on a tenant-scoped table without a tenant filter, any `subprocess` with `shell=True`). Secret scanning with push protection so a key never reaches the remote in the first place. DAST with the OWASP ZAP baseline scan against an ephemeral environment for headers, cookie flags and low-hanging misconfiguration. The gate policy is the senior part: block the merge on new HIGH findings introduced by the diff, report-only on the pre-existing backlog, allow a documented, expiring, reviewer-approved suppression, and never a global `nosec` - a scanner everyone ignores is worse than no scanner because it manufactures false assurance.

resource.label: GitHub Docs: Code security (code scanning, secret scanning, Dependabot)

subtopics.name: A09 Logging and monitoring: making an attack visible
subtopics.learn: Decide what a security event is in your system and make it queryable: authentication success and failure with actor, source IP and user agent; authorization denials (a 403 spike from one principal across many object ids is IDOR probing in progress); privilege and role changes; token issuance and revocation; data export and bulk read; and admin actions. Emit structured JSON with a trace id so a security event joins the same trace as the request (build on OpenTelemetry from topic 21), keep an append-only audit trail with an integrity guarantee for regulated tenants, and set retention to survive the typical months-long dwell time. Equally important, log what you must never log: passwords, tokens, full card numbers, PII in URLs (which land in access logs and Referer headers), and raw prompts containing customer data. Then write two alerts and prove they fire against your own traffic.

resource.label: OWASP Top 10 2021: A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

subtopics.name: Find, score, fix and regression-test one real issue in your own stack
subtopics.learn: Turn the lab skills on Dokeo and DefenderMate and go until you have a genuine finding - most likely a missing tenant predicate, a mass-assignment field, a reflected CORS origin, or a JWT decode without audience validation. Write it up the way a customer's security team expects: title, affected endpoint and commit, severity with an explicit CVSS v3.1 vector string and a sentence on why environmental metrics adjust it for your deployment, minimal reproduction as a copy-pasteable `curl`, evidence, impact in business terms, remediation, and detection guidance. Then fix it, and write the test that would have caught it - a pytest case that authenticates as tenant B and asserts a 403/404 on tenant A's object - and confirm it fails on the vulnerable commit and passes on the fix. A finding without a regression test is a fix that will regress within two releases.

resource.label: FIRST: CVSS v3.1 Specification Document

outcomes: You can complete the PortSwigger apprentice and practitioner labs across access control, authentication, JWT, OAuth, SQL injection, XSS, SSRF, CSRF, XXE and business logic, and produce a lab completion list as evidence.

You can take an unfamiliar API's OpenAPI spec and, within an hour, produce an authorization matrix of endpoint x role x tenant with the identity-swap test result in every cell, and name the highest-risk three routes.
You can exploit and then correctly fix a cross-tenant IDOR in your own code, and ship a pytest regression test that fails on the vulnerable commit and passes on the patched one.

You can forge a JWT four different ways (alg none, unverified signature, weak HMAC secret, jku/kid injection) and audit any codebase's decode calls for algorithm pinning, audience, issuer and expiry in a single grep-driven pass.

You can write a CVSS v3.1 vector for a finding, defend the base metrics you chose, and explain how the environmental score changes for a deployment inside a customer's private VPC versus a public SaaS.

You can explain to a customer's frontend engineer why reflecting the Origin header with credentials enabled is a full authenticated data read, and hand them the correct allowlist implementation in the same conversation.

You can add SAST, secret scanning and a ZAP baseline job to a pipeline with a written gate policy - blocking only diff-introduced HIGH findings, with expiring reviewed suppressions - and state the false-positive rate you measured before enabling the gate.
You can produce a security finding write-up that a customer's security team accepts without a follow-up call: reproduction, impact in business language, remediation, and detection guidance.
failureModes: A tenant-scoped endpoint filters by primary key only because 'the ORM session already has the tenant', row-level security was never enabled on that one table, and a customer analyst enumerating sequential document ids reads another business unit's contracts for six weeks before anyone notices.

The edge proxy and the application normalise paths differently, so an authorization middleware that protects `/admin/` never sees a request to `/admin%2fusers` or `/Admin/users`, and the whole admin surface is reachable unauthenticated behind a rule that looks correct in code review.

CORS was loosened to reflect any Origin with credentials during an on-site integration to unblock a customer's dev server, the change shipped in a hotfix branch with no ticket, and it stays in production until an external pentest finds it.

A JWT is validated for signature but not for `aud` and `iss`, so a token minted by the customer's staging IdP - or by a different application sharing the same identity provider - authenticates successfully against production.

A 'import from URL' document feature is deployed onto a node group where IMDSv1 was left enabled for a legacy agent, turning a low-severity SSRF into instance-role credential theft and an incident that involves the customer's cloud security team.

A dependency is pinned by floating tag in the Dockerfile, the nightly rebuild pulls a new transitive package with a known RCE, and because the SBOM is generated only on tagged releases nobody can answer 'which running images are affected' for two days.

Login rate limiting is enforced at the ALB per source IP, but the same authentication endpoint is reachable through an internal service-mesh route that bypasses the edge entirely, so credential stuffing from inside the cluster succeeds with no lockouts and no alert.
interviewQuestions: Two weeks before go-live, the customer's security team returns a pentest report with fourteen findings against your deployment. Walk me through how you triage it in the next twenty-four hours, which findings you push back on and how, and what you tell their CISO on the call.

Design authorization for a multi-tenant API where enterprise customers have nested org units, delegated admins and shared read-only collaborators. Where exactly is the check enforced, how do you make it impossible for a new endpoint to forget it, and how would you prove to an auditor that no IDOR exists?

Users occasionally see another tenant's data on the dashboard, but only under load and never reproducibly. Walk me through your investigation - what are the candidate mechanisms, and what would you instrument first?

Explain precisely what breaks in each of these three cases and how the exploit differs: a JWT library called with signature verification disabled, a service that accepts `alg: none`, and a service where the `kid` header is used to look up a key from disk without sanitisation.

Your product takes a customer-supplied URL and fetches the document. Enumerate every way that becomes SSRF, then tell me what a real fix looks like in an AWS deployment - not the regex, the architecture.
You find a stored XSS in a customer's production instance at 4pm on a Friday. What happens in the next hour, who do you tell, and what determines whether you hotfix or roll back?

How would you add security testing to a delivery pipeline for a team that will absolutely disable anything noisy? Be specific about what blocks a merge, what is report-only, how suppressions work, and how you would measure whether the gate is earning its keep.
proofOfWork: Publish an internal-pentest dossier repository for Dokeo and DefenderMate that reads like a professional engagement rather than a lab notebook. It contains: a scoped test plan mapped to OWASP ASVS Level 2 controls with each control marked pass, fail or not-applicable and a one-line justification; a generated authorization matrix of every endpoint crossed with every role and both seeded tenants, produced by a committed script that authenticates as each principal, replays each request and records the status code, so the matrix is regenerable on any commit rather than hand-typed; at least one genuine finding written up with a CVSS v3.1 vector string, a copy-pasteable `curl` reproduction, evidence, business impact and remediation; the patch itself as a linked pull request; and a pytest regression test proving the fix, demonstrated by a short recording or CI log showing the test red on the vulnerable commit and green on the patched one. Add the CI wiring that keeps it true - Semgrep with at least two custom rules written for your own footguns, secret scanning with push protection, a ZAP baseline scan against an ephemeral environment, and a documented gate policy explaining exactly what blocks a merge and how suppressions expire - plus a one-page `SECURITY.md` covering the disclosure contact, supported versions and expected response times, which is the document every enterprise procurement review asks for.
